<!-- ex-1: body_md -->
Let $x=(x_1,\dots,x_{n+1})\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Define
\[q(x)=(x_1+ix_2)^k.\]
The restriction of $q$ to $\mathbb{S}^n$, still denoted by $q$, is in $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$, and is called a highest weight spherical harmonic. Following \cite{B2, Ha1}, we also call it a Gaussian beam. It is known that
\[\frac{\|q\|_{L^p(\mathbb{S}^n)}}{\|q\|_{L^2(\mathbb{S}^n)}}\approx k^{\frac{n-1}{4}-\frac{n-1}{2p}}.\]
See Sogge \cite[Theorem 4.1]{So1}. That is, highest weight spherical harmonics saturate the $L^p$ estimates \eqref{eq:Sogge} for all $2<p\le p_n$.
<!-- end ex-1 -->
<!-- ex-2: body_md -->
Let $\{Y_j\}_{j=1}^{N_k}$ be an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$. Consider the reproducing kernel in $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kernel}
K(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^{N_k}Y_j(x)\overline{Y_j(y)}.
\end{equation}
The zonal harmonic with pole $x$ is defined as
\[Z_x(y)=\frac{K(y,x)}{\sqrt{K(x,x)}}\quad\text{for }y\in\mathbb{S}^n.\]
It is known that, for $p_n\le p\le\infty$,
\[\frac{\left\|Z_x\right\|_{L^p(\mathbb{S}^n)}}{\left\|Z_x\right\|_{L^2(\mathbb{S}^n)}}\approx k^{\frac{n-1}{2}-\frac np}.\]
See Sogge \cite[Theorem 4.1]{So1}. That is, zonal harmonics saturate the $L^p$ estimates \eqref{eq:Sogge} for all $p_n\le p\le\infty$.
<!-- end ex-2 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:MaxSH2}
For all sufficiently large $k$, there is an orthonormal set $\{u_j\}_{j=1}^M\subset\mathbb{SH}_k^2$ such that $M\ge\left\lfloor\frac{2k+1}{400}\right\rfloor$ and
\[\left\|u_j\right\|_{L^p(\mathbb{S}^2)}\approx k^{\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2p}}\quad\text{for all }j=1,\dots,M\text{ and }2<p\le6.\]
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:MaxSHhigh}
For each integer $k\ge1$, there is an orthonormal basis $\{u_j\}_{j=1}^{N_k}$ of $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$ such that
\[\left\|u_j\right\|_{L^p(\mathbb{S}^n)}\approx k^{\frac{n-1}{2}-\frac np}\quad\text{for all }j=1,\dots,N_k\text{ and }p_n\le p\le\infty.\]
Here, the implicit constants depend only on $n$ and $p$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:MaxSHlow}
For each integer $k\ge1$, there is an orthonormal basis $\{u_j\}_{j=1}^{N_k}$ of $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$ such that
\[\left\|u_j\right\|_{L^p(\mathbb{S}^n)}\approx k^{\frac{n-1}{4}-\frac{n-1}{2p}}\quad\text{for all }j=1,\dots,N_k\text{ and }2<p\le p_n.\]
Here, the implicit constants depend only on $n$ and $p$.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:HWnorm}
Let $1\le r<\infty$. Then
\[\left\|Q\right\|_{L^r(\mathbb{S}^n)}\approx k^{\frac{n-1}{4}-\frac{n-1}{2r}}.\]
Here, the implicit constants depend on $n$ and $r$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Write
\[x=\left(\rho\cos\theta,\rho\sin\theta,\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,\omega\right),\quad\text{where }0\le\rho\le1, 0\le\theta<2\pi,\omega\in\mathbb{S}^{n-2}.\]
Up to a constant depending only on $n$, the volume form on $\mathbb{S}^n$ is
\[\rho\left(1-\rho^2\right)^{\frac{n-3}{2}}\,d\rho d\theta d\omega,\]
where $d\omega$ is the volume form on $\mathbb{S}^{n-2}$ (the counting measure on $\mathbb{S}^0=\{\pm1\}$ if $n=2$). Since $\operatorname{Re} q(x)=\rho^k\cos(k\theta)$ and $\int_0^{2\pi}|\cos(k\theta)|^r\,d\theta$ is independent of $k$, we have
\[\left\|\operatorname{Re} q\right\|_{L^r(\mathbb{S}^n)}^r\approx\int_0^1\rho^{kr+1}\left(1-\rho^2\right)^{\frac{n-3}{2}}\,d\rho=\frac12B\left(\frac{kr}{2}+1,\frac{n-1}{2}\right)\approx k^{-\frac{n-1}{2}},\]
where $B$ is the Beta function and we substituted $s=\rho^2$. Hence, $\left\|\operatorname{Re} q\right\|_{L^r(\mathbb{S}^n)}\approx k^{-\frac{n-1}{2r}}$ for all $1\le r<\infty$. In particular, $\left\|\operatorname{Re} q\right\|_{L^2(\mathbb{S}^n)}\approx k^{-\frac{n-1}{4}}$, which proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:HWframe}
We have
\[\int_{\mathrm{SO}(n+1)}Q_R\otimes Q_R\,dR=\frac{1}{N_k}\mathrm{I}\]
as an operator on $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$. Consequently, for every $\eta>0$, there are $M_0\ge N_k$ rotations $R_1,\dots,R_{M_0}$, not necessarily distinct, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HWframe}
\left\|\sum_{j=1}^{M_0}Q_{R_j}\otimes Q_{R_j}\right\|\le(1+\eta)\frac{M_0}{N_k}.
\end{equation}
Here, $\|\cdot\|$ is the operator norm on $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For the first statement, see Jakobson--Zelditch \cite[Section 3]{JZ}. We provide a short proof for completeness. Denote the operator on the left-hand side of the first equality by $T$. For $S\in\mathrm{SO}(n+1)$, the map $U_S:u\mapsto u\left(S^{-1}\cdot\right)$ is orthogonal on $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$, and $U_SQ_R=Q_{SR}$. Hence,
\[U_S\left(Q_R\otimes Q_R\right)U_S^{-1}=Q_{SR}\otimes Q_{SR},\]
and the invariance of $dR$ gives $U_STU_S^{-1}=T$. That is, the symmetric operator $T$ commutes with all rotations, so each eigenspace of $T$ is invariant under rotations. Since $n\ge2$, the real vector space $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$ is irreducible under the action of $\mathrm{SO}(n+1)$, because its complexification, the space of complex-valued spherical harmonics of degree $k$, is irreducible. Therefore, $T=c\mathrm{I}$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Taking the trace and using $\|Q_R\|_{L^2(\mathbb{S}^n)}=1$, we obtain $c=N_k^{-1}$. 

For the second statement, since $\mathrm{SO}(n+1)$ is compact and $R\mapsto Q_R\otimes Q_R$ is continuous, we approximate the integral in operator norm by a finite sum $\sum_ja_jQ_{R_j}\otimes Q_{R_j}$ (for instance, by partitioning $\mathrm{SO}(n+1)$ into finitely many Borel sets of small diameter and positive measure), where $a_j>0$ and $\sum_ja_j=1$, such that
\[\left\|\sum_ja_jQ_{R_j}\otimes Q_{R_j}-\frac{1}{N_k}\mathrm{I}\right\|<\frac{\eta}{2N_k}.\]
We then approximate the $a_j$ by positive rational numbers $a_j'$ with $\sum_ja_j'=1$ and $\sum_j|a_j-a_j'|<\frac{\eta}{2N_k}$. Since $\|Q_R\otimes Q_R\|=1$, replacing $a_j$ by $a_j'$ changes the finite sum by less than $\frac{\eta}{2N_k}$ in operator norm. Writing $a_j'=\frac{m_j}{M_0}$ with $m_j\in\mathbb{N}$ and $M_0=\sum_jm_j$, repeating each rotation $R_j$ exactly $m_j$ times, and relabeling, we obtain
\[\left\|\frac{1}{M_0}\sum_{j=1}^{M_0}Q_{R_j}\otimes Q_{R_j}-\frac{1}{N_k}\mathrm{I}\right\|<\frac{\eta}{N_k}.\]
This gives \eqref{eq:HWframe}. By repeating each rotation the same number of times if necessary, we may assume that $M_0\ge N_k$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:grad}
Let $u\in\mathbb{SH}_k^n$. Then
\[\left\|\nabla u\right\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{S}^n)}\le\sqrt{k(k+n-1)N_k}\,\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{S}^n)}\le Ck^{\frac{n+1}{2}}\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{S}^n)}.\]
Here, $C=C(n)\ge1$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $\{Y_j\}_{j=1}^{N_k}$ be a real-valued orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$. Set
\[G(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{N_k}\left|\nabla Y_j(x)\right|^2\quad\text{for }x\in\mathbb{S}^n.\]
Any other real-valued orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$ is of the form $\{\sum_lO_{jl}Y_l\}_{j=1}^{N_k}$ for an orthogonal matrix $O$, so $G$ does not depend on the choice of the basis. For $R\in\mathrm{SO}(n+1)$, applying this to the basis $\{Y_j(R^{-1}\cdot)\}_{j=1}^{N_k}$ and using that $R$ is an isometry of $\mathbb{S}^n$, we obtain $G(R^{-1}x)=G(x)$. Hence, $G$ is constant, and
\[G(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{N_k}\int_{\mathbb{S}^n}\left|\nabla Y_j(y)\right|^2\,dy=\sum_{j=1}^{N_k}\left\langle\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^n}Y_j,Y_j\right\rangle=k(k+n-1)N_k\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{S}^n.\]
Now write $u=\sum_ja_jY_j$, so that $\sum_ja_j^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{S}^n)}^2$. For $x\in\mathbb{S}^n$ and a unit tangent vector $\xi\in T_x\mathbb{S}^n$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
\[\left|\nabla u(x)\cdot\xi\right|=\left|\sum_{j=1}^{N_k}a_j\,\nabla Y_j(x)\cdot\xi\right|\le\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{S}^n)}\sqrt{G(x)}=\sqrt{k(k+n-1)N_k}\,\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{S}^n)}.\]
Taking the supremum over $\xi$ and $x$ gives the first inequality. The second one follows from \eqref{eq:dim}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:RI}
Let $0<\delta<1$ and $L:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be a linear map. Suppose that $v_1,\dots,v_m\in\mathbb{R}^d$ satisfy $\sum_{j=1}^mv_jv_j^\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{I}$, where $\mathrm{I}$ is the identity matrix. Then there is a subset $J\subset\{1,\dots,m\}$ with
\[|J|\ge\left\lfloor\frac{\delta^2\|L\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2}{\|L\|^2}\right\rfloor\]
such that $\{Lv_j\}_{j\in J}$ is linearly independent and
\[\mu_{\min}\left(\sum_{j\in J}\left(Lv_j\right)\left(Lv_j\right)^\mathrm{t}\right)>\frac{(1-\delta)^2\|L\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2}{m},\]
where $\mu_{\min}$ is computed on $\operatorname{span}\{Lv_j\}_{j\in J}$.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
Let $t\in\mathbb{N}$. A finite subset $\{x_1,\dots,x_M\}\subset\mathbb{S}^n$ is called a spherical $t$-design if
\[\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^MP\left(x_j\right)=\int_{\mathbb{S}^n}P(y)\,dy\]
for every polynomial $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ of degree at most $t$, restricted to $\mathbb{S}^n$.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:BRV}
There is a constant $c_n>0$ such that for every $t\in\mathbb{N}$ and every $M\ge c_nt^n$, there is a spherical $t$-design in $\mathbb{S}^n$ consisting of $M$ points.
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:frame}
Let $\{x_1,\dots,x_M\}\subset\mathbb{S}^n$ be a spherical $2k$-design. Then
\[\sum_{j=1}^MZ_{x_j}\otimes Z_{x_j}=\frac{M}{N_k}\mathrm{I}\]
as an operator on $\mathbb{SH}_k^n$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $u\in\mathbb{SH}_k^n$. Then $u^2$ is the restriction to $\mathbb{S}^n$ of a polynomial of degree $2k$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Hence, by \eqref{eq:eval} and the spherical design property,
\[\left\langle\left(\sum_{j=1}^MZ_{x_j}\otimes Z_{x_j}\right)u,u\right\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^M\left\langle u,Z_{x_j}\right\rangle^2=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{j=1}^Mu(x_j)^2=\frac{M}{N_k}\int_{\mathbb{S}^n}u(y)^2\,dy=\frac{M}{N_k}\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{S}^n)}^2.\]
Since the operator on the left-hand side is symmetric, the lemma follows.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:completion}
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a real Hilbert space of dimension $N$. Suppose that $\{u_j\}_{j=1}^M$ is an orthonormal set in $\mathcal{H}$ with $M\ge\frac N2$. Assume that $w_1,\dots,w_M\in\mathcal{H}$ satisfy
\[\left\langle u_j,w_j\right\rangle\ge c>0\quad\text{for all }j=1,\dots,M.\]
Then there is an orthonormal basis $\{v_j\}_{j=1}^N$ of $\mathcal{H}$ such that, for each $j=1,\dots,N$, there is an index $l(j)\in\{1,\dots,M\}$ with
\[\left\langle v_j,w_{l(j)}\right\rangle\ge\frac{c}{\sqrt2}.\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Complete $\{u_j\}_{j=1}^M$ to an orthonormal basis by adding $h_1,\dots,h_{N-M}$. Since $N-M\le M$, we can pair $h_i$ with $u_i$ for $i=1,\dots,N-M$. For each pair, set
\[a_i=\left\langle u_i,w_i\right\rangle,\quad b_i=\left\langle h_i,w_i\right\rangle,\quad r_i=\sqrt{a_i^2+b_i^2}\ge c.\]
Define
\[s_i=\frac{a_iu_i+b_ih_i}{r_i}\quad\text{and}\quad t_i=\frac{-b_iu_i+a_ih_i}{r_i}.\]
Then $s_i$ and $t_i$ are orthonormal and span the same subspace as $u_i$ and $h_i$. Moreover,
\[\left\langle s_i,w_i\right\rangle=r_i\quad\text{and}\quad\left\langle t_i,w_i\right\rangle=0.\]
Consequently, the two vectors
\[v_i^+=\frac{s_i+t_i}{\sqrt2}\quad\text{and}\quad v_i^-=\frac{s_i-t_i}{\sqrt2}\]
are orthonormal and satisfy
\[\left\langle v_i^+,w_i\right\rangle=\left\langle v_i^-,w_i\right\rangle=\frac{r_i}{\sqrt2}\ge\frac{c}{\sqrt2}.\]
Replacing each pair $u_i,h_i$ by $v_i^+,v_i^-$ and retaining the unpaired $u_j$ gives the required orthonormal basis.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
